catalog_quote: The phonological word, with the couplet as its basis, may have several syllables either preceding or following the couplet. Word stress is on the first syllable of the couplet. In examples, the couplet precedes space or hyphen (-). káha do / káha-viʔató it (machine) does good / kònàkàhà-ñá she didn't do it [p. 21] ... One further morphophonemic process takes place when /i/ or /e/ are postposed to a nonverbal couplet. When these vowel clusters are formed by the postposing of single-vowel enclitic person markers, the stress of the couplet is shifted to the syllable immediately preceding that of the enclitic, and the tone of the syllable receiving the stress becomes high. This has the effect of reformulating the last syllable of the original couplet as the first syllable of a new couplet with the enclitic as its second syllable. hàtà back / hàtáì my back ... sweep_summary: Silacayoapan Mixtec (sila1250) is not in the catalog. The single works with stress in the title, Carroll 2015 (UCSD PhD, Ixpantepec Nieves variety, Glottolog-linked to sila1250), was already held by the project (downloaded by the mixt1425 search from eScholarship/CORE) and was read: it is a first-hand phonological and acoustic study giving fixed default stress on the first syllable of the bimoraic root couplet (trochaic foot aligned to the root; prefixes/clitics never stressed; correlates duration, intensity, periodicity), pp. 98-99. Through its bibliography the primary description of Silacayoapan proper, North & Shields 1977 (SIL PIL 54, pp. 21-33; data from San Jerónimo Progreso), was located in the Merrifield 1977 volume already held by the project from the sanm1301 search; pp. 21 and 31-33 were scanned. It states 'Word stress is on the first syllable of the couplet' (p. 21) with a stress-plus-H-tone shift onto the couplet's second syllable before single-vowel person enclitics on non-verb couplets (p. 31, Rule 4), which Carroll re-analyses as a perceptual effect. Both first-hand sources agree on root-couplet-initial stress; nothing remains unread. only direct download/automated download were used (Glottolog record 569742 confirmed the sila1250 link; eScholarship returned empty by automated download, SIL and DuckDuckGo downloads were blocked).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the first syllable of the couplet, i.e. the bimoraic (usually disyllabic) root that forms the nucleus of the phonological word; prefixes, proclitics and enclitics before or after the couplet are unstressed (Shields 1976 ms p. 1: 'Word affixes do not carry stress'), so stress is root-initial rather than word-initial (e.g. kàha 'do', kòna-kàha-ñá 'she didn't do it'). One morphologically conditioned shift: a single-vowel enclitic person marker (1s /i/ ~ /e/) on a nonverbal couplet moves the stress to the couplet's second syllable, which also takes high tone (hàtà 'back' > hàtá-ì 'my back'), reforming the couplet with the enclitic. Carroll 2015 (Ixpantepec Nieves, same ISO grouping) finds the same root-initial trochaic stress, fixed under affixation and cliticisation, with duration, intensity and periodicity as correlates, and argues the apparent enclitic shift is a perceptual effect of a HL contour plus vowel fusion, not a change of stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift under single-vowel enclitic person markers on nonverbal couplets (North & Shields 1977:31, Rule 4); Carroll 2015:100-101 adds that lexicalised prefix+root trimoraic words in Nieves stress the etymological root, and irregular verbs can stress a prefix. Carroll 2015:91, 100 n. 5 contests the Silacayoapan shift as a perceptual effect.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (couplet plus any preceding or following syllables), in citation forms and phrase examples; North & Shields describe stress as the mark of the couplet within the word, not phrase-level prominence. Carroll 2015 is a word-prosody study with acoustic measurements.
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement (North & Shields 1977; also Shields 1976 ms and Shields 1995 ms) describes the Mixtec of San Jerónimo Progreso, Municipio Silacayoapan (Josserand 1983's Western Baja area), the eponymous variety of sila1250 / ISO mks. Carroll 2015 describes Ixpantepec Nieves, a Southern Baja variety that ISO/Glottolog fold into mks (Carroll 2015:7 treats it as a separate dialect group); Cortés et al. 2023, Weller et al. 2025 and Mantenuto 2020 describe San Sebastián del Monte, which Glottolog also files under sila1250. None of the three has its own glottocode. The two first-hand descriptions agree on root(couplet)-initial stress; they differ on whether the 1s vocalic enclitic shifts stress (North & Shields: yes; Carroll: no).

new_statements.reading: Fixed word stress on the first syllable of the bimoraic root couplet (initial stress of the root, not of the phonological word: pre-couplet prefixes/proclitics and post-couplet enclitics are unstressed). One morphologically conditioned exception: a single-vowel person enclitic (/i/ 1s, /e/) on a non-verb couplet moves stress one syllable rightward onto the couplet's second syllable, which also takes H tone. Carroll 2015 (pp. 98-99), the fuller first-hand study of the Ixpantepec Nieves variety under the same glottocode, confirms couplet-initial (root-initial) trochaic stress with acoustic evidence and argues the enclitic 'shift' is a perceptual effect of tone contour and vowel fusion rather than a stress shift. Both sources agree on the default: stress on the first syllable of the root couplet.

sources.quote: Nieves Mixtec maintains a close parallelism between the morphological structure and the prosodic structure. In the minimal word, consisting only of a bimoraic root, stress falls on the first syllable as in (4.20). [...] The position of stress is fixed, as it does not change with the addition of monomoraic functional morphemes. [...] In contrast to the stress system described for Silacayoapan Mixtec (North & Shields 1977), mentioned in §4.2, in Nieves Mixtec the stress is maintained on the first syllable of the root even when the 1s enclitic /=ì/ is added to the root, as in (4.25).
